title: Uisdean begins to write beyond the weather
summary: In his second spring keeping the daybook of Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Uisdean mac Lachlainn writes down more than the wind and the oil for the first time: that a farmer of his acquaintance ploughs alone, with none of the hands who worked beside him the year before.

title: The draft read at Baile chrom
summary: An Togail is read at the market cross of Baile chrom, first in the humans' tongue and then in Dia-thìris by a clerk who stumbles over the numbers. It falls hardest on the coast and hill villages; the concession farms to the north, worked by the strangers' own people, send no one.

title: The first harvest short
summary: The harvest round Baile chrom comes in at less than half the carts of the year before, the fields sown thin for want of hands and beaten further by two summer storms. Uisdean counts the carts against his own earlier tally and finds the shortfall for himself.

title: Mòr nic Aonghais sends her son south
summary: At Doire ghlas, a woman named Mòr nic Aonghais walks her fourteen-year-old son as far as the boundary stone and no further, by the coast's custom, and sends him to the camps for A' Chompanaidh's ration rather than keep him at a table with too little on it.

title: The kitchen at Inis mhin's harbour
summary: With its seed corn eaten and no crop sown, Inis mhin is fed through the second winter of the hunger by Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's kitchen at the harbour, which serves three hundred a day on fish broth and biscuit brought by sea from Cathair gheal.

title: The grain-pits of Seann Bhrenn opened
summary: The custodians of Seann Bhrenn lever open the sealed grain-pits of the Age of Sinnsearachd on the chalk hill above the town, unopened in living memory and kept against a need no one thought would come, and find in them only the dust of grain a hundred generations gone.

title: Anne Colby's letter to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir
summary: With the relief ship idle at anchor, Anne Colby writes to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir at Ros dhomhain asking only who should be told to unload it. Eleven days pass before an answer that names no one and settles nothing, noting only that Àrd-mhaor Tolley has heard her concern.

title: The relief ship unloaded without an order
summary: After a month idle in the roads at Ros dhomhain, the relief ship's holds are opened at last when a clerk of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and a clerk of A' Chompanaidh set men to the work themselves, without waiting for either office to settle the dispute between them.

title: Anne Colby takes the kitchen at Baile chrom
summary: Anne Colby goes north to Baile chrom to run Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's kitchen in a net-shed by the harbour, and keeps it through the worst of the hunger on the relief ship's grain and whatever the boats can add to it.

title: Anne Colby's private roll of names
summary: At the Baile chrom kitchen Anne Colby keeps a book of her own, apart from Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's, writing every name she feeds and crossing it through, gently, in the corner of the page, whenever that person does not come again.

title: Uisdean's hand on the valve
summary: In the second winter of the hunger, Uisdean mac Lachlainn climbs to the lamp of Taigh-solais Baile chrom and stands a long while with his hand on the oil valve, weighing whether to let the light fail. He writes the thought into the daybook and lets the lamp burn on.

title: An Togail read ended at Baile chrom
summary: The clerk who first read An Togail at the market cross of Baile chrom returns to read that it is set aside in the famine districts, two harvests after the failure it caused. The custodians note it is not repealed, only set by, and expect no more of it.

title: Cnoc mhòr walks south together
summary: Before An Togail's suspension is even drafted, the whole village of Cnoc mhòr in the north walks south to take A' Chompanaidh's ration and its work, old carried and young walking, leaving its doors unbarred behind it in the manner of a people who mean to return.

title: The grass in Cnoc mhòr's street
summary: A carter passing through empty Cnoc mhòr some weeks after its people leave finds every door shut but unbarred, and grass already coming up between the stones of the street, a sign that reaches the kitchen at Baile chrom before the village itself is spoken of again.
